title: Collapse Neighboring Anagrams
statement:
You get a list of lowercase words. Two words are anagrams if one is a rearrangement of the other's letters, using every letter exactly as often.

Repeat this until it no longer applies: find a position i > 0 where words[i] is an anagram of the word directly before it, and delete words[i].

Return the list that remains. The final result does not depend on which deletions you make first.

examples.why: "stop" and "pots" collapse into "tops", "act" into "cat". The last "tops" stays: its neighbor is now "cat". Removing anagrams anywhere in the list would wrongly drop it.
"ab" and "ba" are anagrams, but they are never neighbors.
"abcc" has an extra c, so it is not an anagram of either neighbor, and it keeps "abc" and "cab" apart.

constraints: words[i] contains only lowercase English letters
hints: Deleting a word makes its anagram neighbor the new neighbor of the next word. What do you notice about that neighbor?
Anagrams form groups: if b is an anagram of a, and c is an anagram of b, then c is an anagram of a. So comparing with the last kept word is the same as comparing with the original neighbor.
Walk the list once, keeping words[i] only if it is not an anagram of words[i − 1]. Compare anagrams by sorted letters or by letter counts.

explain.intuition:
Deletions chain: in ["tops", "stop", "pots"], deleting "stop" puts "pots" next to "tops". But being anagrams is transitive, so "pots" is an anagram of "tops" exactly when it is an anagram of "stop". That means every word can be judged by its original left neighbor, and a single left-to-right pass is enough.

To test two words, compare a canonical form: the letters sorted, or a 26-slot count of letters. It is the same move as normalizing keys before comparing them.
steps: For each i ≥ 1, compute the sorted-letters key of words[i] and of words[i − 1].
Return the kept words in order.
pitfalls: Removing every word that is an anagram of any earlier word, not just of its neighbor. The last "tops" in the first example must stay.
Treating words with the same set of letters as anagrams: "aab" and "abb" use the same letters with different counts.
Deleting from an array while iterating over it by index, which skips the element after each deletion.

complexity.time: O(n · L log L) with sorting, O(n · L) with counts

solutions.title: Simulate the deletions
solutions.idea: Repeatedly scan for a word that is an anagram of the word before it and splice it out, until no such pair is left.

solutions.title: One pass against the original neighbor
solutions.idea: Anagrams are transitive, so a word is deleted exactly when it is an anagram of the word originally before it.

followups: Words can be up to 100 000 letters long. How do you compare them without sorting?
Delete a word when it is an anagram of any word still in the list. What changes?
lcTitle: Find Resultant Array After Removing Anagrams
